summary: Defines MIME Object Security Services, a protocol that uses the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted framework to add digital signatures and encryption to MIME objects. It was standards-track but is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: MIME tells an email program how to package a message, but it says nothing about protecting it. MOSS adds two protections that work on any kind of message: a digital signature and encryption. A user needs one pair of keys, one kept secret and one shared.

subtitle: Signing and encrypting MIME email with plain public key pairs, no certificates required.

tldr.problem: MIME defines how to package the contents of a mail message but offers no security services, and the older PEM scheme covered only text messages and required every user to hold a certificate.
tldr.mechanism: MOSS fills the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted framework with one-line control headers. Originator-ID, MIC-Info, DEK-Info, Recipient-ID and Key-Info carry the signature value or the encrypted data encrypting key, and each signature uses a hash sealed with the originator's private key.
tldr.outcome: Any single or multi-part MIME object can be signed or encrypted, and a user needs only a public and private key pair. The RFC was a Standards Track document from October 1995 and is now Historic.

today: RFC 1848 is a Historic RFC from October 1995. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The framework it fills in, RFC 1847, defines the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted content types that MOSS uses.

sections.title: What MOSS Adds to MIME
sections.content:
MIME, an acronym for Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, defines the format of the contents of Internet mail messages and provides for multi-part textual and non-textual message bodies, but it does not provide for the application of security services. PEM, an acronym for Privacy Enhanced Mail, defines message encryption and message authentication procedures for text-based electronic mail messages using a certificate-based key management mechanism, and it is limited by applying security services to text messages only.

MOSS, the MIME Object Security Services, is based in large part on the PEM protocol as defined in RFC 1421. It uses the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted framework of RFC 1847 to apply digital signature and encryption services to MIME objects. The services are offered through end-to-end cryptography between an originator and a recipient at the application layer. Asymmetric (public key) cryptography supports the digital signature service and the encryption key management, and symmetric (secret key) cryptography supports the encryption service.

To use MOSS, a user needs at least one public and private key pair. The public key must be made available to the users with whom secure communication is desired, and the private key must not be disclosed to any other user. The originator's private key signs MIME objects and a recipient verifies the signature with the originator's public key. A recipient's public key encrypts the data encrypting key that encrypts the MIME object, and the recipient's private key decrypts that key so the object can be decrypted. The security considerations section of the RFC says only that the entire document is about security.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME tells an email program how to package a message, but it does not say how to protect it. MOSS adds two protections that work on any kind of message: a digital signature and encryption. A user needs one pair of keys, one kept secret and one shared.

sections.title: Signing a MIME Object
sections.content:
Signing a MIME body part takes four steps. The body part must be canonicalized, the digital signature and the other control information must be generated, the control information must be embodied in a MIME content type, and the control information and the data must be embodied in a multipart/signed content type.

Canonicalization has two steps. The body part is first converted to a form that is unambiguously representable on as many different computers as possible, and MIME's 7bit form is the one chosen for this. Content that is not already 7bit must be encoded with an appropriate MIME content transfer encoding, such as quoted-printable or base64, and a Content-Transfer-Encoding header added. The second step converts the local line delimiter to the two character sequence CRLF, because the originator and the recipient have to use the same one. The conversion is used only to compute the signature: an originator applies it before computing the signature but transfers the data without it, because SMTP servers may change the line delimiter in transit, and a recipient applies it again before recomputing the hash.

The signature itself is a hash of the prepared data, encrypted with the originator's private key. The control information is a set of one-line RFC 822 headers, and folding a header value onto continuation lines is forbidden. The complete set is Version:, which indicates which version of the MOSS protocol the remaining headers represent, Originator-ID:, which identifies the private key used to create the signature and the public key to verify it, and MIC-Info:, which carries the signature value as a comma separated list of the hash algorithm, the signature algorithm and the signature. Every use of the service emits exactly one Version header, always first, and at least one pair of Originator-ID and MIC-Info headers in that order.

The two parts are then placed in a multipart/signed body part. Its required protocol parameter is set to application/moss-signature, the signed body part becomes the first part, and the second part is labelled application/moss-signature and holds the control information. The required micalg parameter is set to the same value used in the MIC-Info header, or to a comma separated list if there is more than one. To verify, a recipient recomputes the hash over the prepared data, decrypts the hash value in the control information with the originator's public key, and compares the two values.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender first rewrites the message into one exact form, so that both sides compute the same fingerprint of it. The sender then seals that fingerprint with the secret key and puts the seal next to the message.

sections.title: Encrypting a MIME Object
sections.content:
Encrypting takes four steps as well. The body part must be in MIME canonical form, the data encrypting key and the other control information must be generated, the control information must be embodied in a MIME content type, and the control information and the encrypted data must be embodied in a multipart/encrypted content type.

The originator creates a data encrypting key and encrypts the data with it. The public key of each recipient is then used to encrypt the data encrypting key. The control information is again a set of one-line RFC 822 headers: exactly one Version: header, exactly one DEK-Info: header naming the algorithm and mode used to encrypt the data along with any cryptographic parameters that may be required, such as initialization vectors, and at least one pair of Recipient-ID: and Key-Info: headers, one pair per recipient, in that order. The Key-Info header carries the data encrypting key encrypted with the recipient's public key.

The multipart/encrypted body part sets its protocol parameter to application/moss-keys. The first body part is labelled application/moss-keys and holds the control information, and the encrypted body part becomes the second body part, labelled application/octet-stream. The RFC tells implementors to always add a Recipient-ID and Key-Info pair for the originator as well, so that a message returned as undelivered can still be read by its sender. A recipient locates the Recipient-ID header that identifies them, uses their private key to decrypt the following Key-Info, and then decrypts the data, which comes back as a MIME body part ready for a MIME agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender makes one random key and locks the message with it. Then the sender locks a copy of that key with each recipient's public key, so only the intended recipients can open it.

sections.title: Identifying People and Their Keys
sections.content:
In PEM, public keys must be embodied in certificates, objects that bind each public key to a distinguished name and are issued by a certification authority, a role expected to be trustworthy because it has procedures to verify the identity of the owner. In MOSS, a user is not required to have a certificate. The Originator-ID and Recipient-ID headers may instead carry an identifier, which has two parts: a name form and a key selector. The combination of the two identifies one public key uniquely.

Three name forms are defined: email addresses, arbitrary strings of at least one character, and distinguished names, the last retained for compatibility with PEM. The name form is chosen and asserted by the user who owns the key pair. The key selector has to be unique with respect to the name form it is used with, and the RFC suggests using a portion, such as the low-order 16 or 32 bits, or all of the actual public key.

There are five identifier types. EN is an email address, STR an arbitrary string, DN a distinguished name, PK the public key itself with an optional name form subset, and IS an issuer name and serial number, kept for compatibility with the older PEM fields. Most identifiers have the form TYPE, KEYSEL, STRING. Naming the public key itself allows encrypted anonymous mail, because a recipient can still tell that repeated messages come from the same key, but a recipient of a PK identifier has to check that the claimed name-to-key association is real.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key gets a label made of a name and a short selector, so a message can say exactly which of your keys it means. The name can be an email address, any text you like, or an X.500 name.

sections.title: Requesting and Sending Key Material
sections.content:
Two content types let users ask for and send key material. application/mosskey-request asks for one of three things: a public key or a certificate chain for a subject, a certificate revocation list chain for an issuer, or the certification of a self-signed certificate. application/mosskey-data returns public keys, certificate chains or certificate revocation list chains. A message can carry several request body parts, and the reply can carry several data body parts, one for each item the responder returns.

The RFC states plainly that it makes no provision for determining the authenticity or accuracy of the data being conveyed. When a public key and its identifier travel this way, nothing prevents the source or an interloper along the path from substituting different values for the key or the identifier. The checking is left to the recipient, and it can be done with certificates, since a certification hierarchy is a well-defined mechanism that supports automatic verification, or by having the source digitally sign the body part it sends.
sections.plainLanguage: A user can mail a note asking for a public key and get one back. But nothing in these messages proves the key really belongs to the sender, so the recipient has to check it separately.

sections.title: How MOSS Differs from PEM
sections.content:
The RFC lists the ways in which MOSS differs from PEM. A user of MOSS needs only a public and private key pair, where PEM required a certificate. MOSS broadens the name forms that may be used to identify a public key, to include arbitrary strings, email addresses and distinguished names. PEM supported only text-based mail whose text had to be in the ASCII character set with CR LF line delimiters, and those restrictions no longer apply. PEM required encryption to be applied only to message bodies that had been signed, while MOSS defines the two services separately so that they may be applied in any order.

MIME already provides the transfer encoding operations that PEM had to include, and the MIME Content-Type headers subsume the PEM Proc-Type and Content-Domain headers. The PEM header fields for certificates and certificate revocation lists are confined to the two new MOSS key management content types, which separates key management from the signature and encryption services. MOSS explicitly excludes symmetric key management, and it requires all data that is digitally signed to be represented in 7bit form.
sections.plainLanguage: MOSS is a more flexible version of PEM. It needs no certificates, it works on any kind of content, and signing and locking can be used separately or together in either order.

data.title: multipart/signed with MOSS
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/signed;
  protocol="application/moss-signature";
  micalg="rsa-md5"; boundary="Signed Message"

--Signed Message
Content-Type: text/plain

This is some example text.
--Signed Message
Content-Type: application/moss-signature

Version: 5
Originator-ID: ID-INFORMATION
MIC-Info: RSA-MD5,RSA,SIGNATURE-INFORMATION
--Signed Message--

data.title: multipart/encrypted with MOSS
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/encrypted;
  protocol="application/moss-keys";
  boundary="Encrypted Message"

--Encrypted Message
Content-Type: application/moss-keys

Version: 5
DEK-Info: DES-CBC,DEK-INFORMATION
Recipient-ID: ID-INFORMATION
Key-Info: RSA,KEY-INFORMATION

--Encrypted Message
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

ENCRYPTED-DATA
--Encrypted Message--
